candidate.blueprint_locator: Health Promotion and Maintenance — prevention and early detection of health problems and assessment of risk factors
candidate.blueprint_topic: Health Promotion and Maintenance — cardiometabolic risk-factor assessment
candidate.educational_objective: Explain why waist circumference complements BMI when assessing excess-adiposity-related cardiometabolic risk.

options.A: Waist circumference is less relevant than BMI and adds no useful adiposity information
options.B: Once BMI is normal, abdominal adiposity no longer contributes to cardiometabolic risk assessment
options.C: A larger waist generally indicates greater lean muscle mass and lower metabolic risk
options.D: Waist circumference provides complementary information about abdominal adiposity and excess-adiposity-related cardiometabolic risk

candidate.rationale: The 2026 AHA/ACC/ADA/ASN CKM guideline recommends assessing both BMI and waist circumference to characterize risk related to excess adiposity. Waist circumference adds information about abdominal adiposity and can identify risk not fully captured by BMI alone. D is correct.
candidate.source_claim_supported: BMI and waist circumference are both recommended because waist circumference provides complementary information about abdominal adiposity and excess-adiposity-related risk.
candidate.source_document_title: 2026 AHA/ACC/ADA/ASN Guideline for the Prevention, Detection, Evaluation, and Management of Cardiovascular-Kidney-Metabolic Syndrome
candidate.source_locator: Professional Heart Daily Top Things to Know, item 6 — assess overweight/obesity and abdominal adiposity with both BMI and waist circumference to characterize excess-adiposity risk
candidate.source_organization: American Heart Association / American College of Cardiology / American Diabetes Association / American Society of Nephrology
candidate.stem: A client has a normal BMI but an elevated waist circumference. Why is the waist measurement still clinically useful in preventive risk assessment?
